question: Which antibody class is the main driver behind severe allergic reactions like anaphylaxis?
explanation: Think of IgE as the trigger-happy antibody! In anaphylaxis, IgE binds to mast cells and sets off a massive allergic chain reaction. [learn more](GST114_U4_T9#GST114_U4_T9_h1)

question: What actually happens when a mast cell 'degranulates' during an allergy attack?

options.A: Antibodies are slowly manufactured inside the bone marrow
options.B: Inflammatory chemicals are rapidly released into the bloodstream
options.C: White blood cells consume and destroy the foreign trigger
options.D: Red blood cells multiply quickly to fight off the allergen

explanation: Mast cells act like tiny storage bags of histamine. When triggered, they pop open and dump their contents directly into your circulation, causing classic allergy symptoms. [learn more](GST114_U4_T9#GST114_U4_T9_h1)

question: Which common medication class is one of the top triggers for hospital-acquired anaphylaxis?
explanation: Penicillin and other beta-lactam drugs are famous culprits. Always double-check a patient's allergy history before giving them! [learn more](GST114_U4_T9#GST114_U4_T9_h2)

question: A patient suddenly collapses after being stung by a bee. What substance did the bee inject to cause this?
explanation: Insect stings deliver venom packed with proteins that can act as powerful allergens in sensitive people. [learn more](GST114_U4_T9#GST114_U4_T9_h2)

question: Which breathing sound is a classic red flag for respiratory involvement in anaphylaxis?
explanation: When airways swell up (stridor) and spasm (wheezing), air has a hard time getting through. This is an urgent airway warning! [learn more](GST114_U4_T9#GST114_U4_T9_h3)

question: A patient eats shrimp, gets hives, swollen lips, and a dangerous drop in blood pressure. What caused the blood pressure to drop so fast?

options.A: Sudden slowing of the electrical heart rhythm
options.C: Rapid clotting of blood inside the major veins
options.D: Severe internal bleeding from the stomach

explanation: Histamine relaxes blood vessels all over the body at once. When they open up too wide, blood pressure plummets—that's distributive shock! [learn more](GST114_U4_T9#GST114_U4_T9_h3)

question: Why must a nurse focus on the ABCDE assessment immediately during suspected anaphylaxis instead of waiting for lab test results?

options.A: Rapid airway closure and shock can cause death within minutes
options.B: Laboratory tests are completely useless for diagnosing allergies
options.C: Skin symptoms always disappear before lab results return
options.D: Hospital protocol forbids drawing blood during emergencies

explanation: Anaphylaxis moves lightning fast. There's no time to wait for lab work when someone's airway is closing up—act first, assess fast! [learn more](GST114_U4_T9#GST114_U4_T9_h4)

question: If a patient shows clear signs of shock after eating an allergen, which classic symptom might actually be completely missing?
explanation: Surprise! Up to 20% of severe anaphylaxis cases don't show any skin rashes or hives. Never rule out anaphylaxis just because the skin looks clear. [learn more](GST114_U4_T9#GST114_U4_T9_h4)

question: What is the absolute golden-standard, first-line drug treatment for acute anaphylaxis?
explanation: Epinephrine is a lifesaver. It quickly constricts blood vessels and opens up airways, reversing the worst effects of anaphylaxis. [learn more](GST114_U4_T9#GST114_U4_T9_h5)

question: Where is the best anatomical site to inject emergency epinephrine?
explanation: The vastus lateralis (mid-outer thigh) absorbs epinephrine the fastest into the bloodstream. Plus, you can even give it right through trousers in a rush! [learn more](GST114_U4_T9#GST114_U4_T9_h5)

question: What exactly is a 'biphasic' anaphylactic reaction?

options.A: A mild skin rash that turns into severe breathing difficulty within minutes
options.B: A sudden allergic response that only affects the skin and digestive system
options.C: A return of symptoms hours after the initial attack without new allergen exposure
options.D: An allergic reaction triggered by two different foods at the exact same time

explanation: A biphasic reaction is like a sneaky second wave. Symptoms come back hours later even though the patient had no new contact with the trigger. [learn more](GST114_U4_T9#GST114_U4_T9_h6)

question: A peanut allergy patient feels completely fine 30 minutes after getting epinephrine and asks to go home immediately. What should the nurse do?

options.A: Perform allergy skin prick testing before allowing the patient to leave
options.B: Explain that prolonged observation is required to watch for secondary symptom flare-ups
options.C: Discharge the patient immediately with a prescription for oral antihistamines
options.D: Administer a second dose of epinephrine just to prevent any future problems

explanation: Don't let them rush off just yet! Because of the risk of biphasic reactions, patients need to stay in the hospital for observation for a few hours. [learn more](GST114_U4_T9#GST114_U4_T9_h6)

question: What is the most crucial instruction for a patient who has just used an epinephrine auto-injector?

options.A: Take a hot shower to wash off any remaining allergen
options.B: Seek immediate emergency medical help at a hospital
options.C: Eat a small meal to restore normal blood sugar levels
options.D: Go to sleep quietly to let the medication take full effect

explanation: Epinephrine buys precious time, but it wears off. Every patient who uses an auto-injector must head straight to the hospital for monitoring. [learn more](GST114_U4_T9#GST114_U4_T9_h7)

question: What practical accessory should individuals with severe, life-threatening allergies wear at all times?
explanation: If a patient collapses and cannot speak, a medical alert bracelet speaks for them, alerting emergency responders instantly. [learn more](GST114_U4_T9#GST114_U4_T9_h7)
